plan: Ten new items; topics checked against all verbal bank passages (a migration-timing inference was dropped because 'Songbird migration notes' already covers it). fragmentary/galvanized WIC, Great Wall sentence function, salmon-nitrogen inference, museum two-gap data, uptalk cross-text, raven planning synthesis (time gap), electric-car concession, Tollund Man modifier, semicolon with 'however'.

passages.title: A partial skeleton
passages.text: The new dinosaur species was described from a single ______ specimen: the skeleton lacked its skull and most of its tail, so researchers could estimate the animal's length only roughly.

passages.title: A decisive speech
passages.text: Before the senator spoke, the bill's supporters had seemed divided and unsure. Her speech ______ them: many who had wavered announced their support the next morning, and the bill passed within the week.

passages.title: Seen from orbit
passages.text: Many people believe that the Great Wall of China can easily be seen from space with the naked eye. Astronauts who have looked for it from low orbit report that it is very hard to pick out. Although the wall is extremely long, it is only a few meters wide and is built from materials close in color to the land around it. Highways and airport runways, which are wider and contrast more with their surroundings, are far easier to spot.

passages.title: Fish in the forest
passages.text: Pacific salmon spend most of their lives in the ocean but return to rivers to spawn and die. Bears catch many of them and often carry the carcasses into the woods to eat. Researchers have found that leaves of trees growing beside salmon streams contain a form of nitrogen that is common in the ocean but rare on land, and that such trees can grow faster than trees of the same species beside streams without salmon. These findings suggest that ______

passages.title: Two kinds of visits
passages.text:
A museum surveyed visitors in four age groups about how they had experienced its collection in the past year.
Age group | Visited in person | Took a virtual tour
18–29 | 45% | 38%
30–49 | 52% | 31%
50–64 | 48% | 22%
65 and older | 55% | 14%
A researcher concluded that the gap between in-person visits and virtual tours is much wider among the oldest visitors than among the youngest.

passages.title: Rising at the end (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
In many varieties of English, some speakers end statements with a rise in pitch, as if asking a question. Critics of this habit, often called uptalk, argue that it signals uncertainty and makes speakers sound less confident than they are.
Text 2
Linguists who have analyzed recorded conversations report that speakers often use this rising pitch on statements they are clearly sure of, such as when giving directions or listing facts. In those settings, the rise seems to work as a check, inviting the listener to signal that they are following.

passages.title: A raven's plan
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In a 2017 study, researchers taught ravens to use a stone tool to open a box containing food.
• Later, with the box out of sight, each raven was offered the tool among several useless objects.
• Most ravens picked the tool and kept it.
• The researchers tested delays of 15 minutes and of 17 hours before returning the box.
• When the box was returned, as much as 17 hours later, the ravens used the tool to open it.
• Planning for a future need is rare among animals.

passages.title: Not quite emission-free
passages.text: Electric cars produce no tailpipe emissions. ______ manufacturing their batteries takes a great deal of energy, much of which still comes from burning fossil fuels, so the cars are not emission-free over their full lives.

passages.title: Found in a bog
passages.text: Excavated from a peat bog in Denmark in 1950, ______ so well preserved that the people who found it first thought they had come upon a recent crime.

passages.title: Delayed reopening
passages.text: The bridge had been scheduled to reopen in ______ repairs to its suspension cables took longer than engineers expected, and it remained closed until August.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: the skeleton lacked its skull and most of its tail
candidates.explanation: The colon explains that the specimen was missing major parts, so it was incomplete: "fragmentary."

B.rationale: A skeleton missing its skull and most of its tail is the opposite of pristine.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests a second, matching specimen; the text says there was a single one.

D.rationale: A dinosaur known from a skeleton is not a living specimen.

hints: What does the text after the colon say about the skeleton?
candidates.remember: The explanation after a colon usually defines the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: many who had wavered announced their support the next morning
candidates.explanation: Wavering supporters were roused to act and the bill passed, so the speech "galvanized" (stirred into action) them.

A.rationale: Supporters who then announced their support were not driven away.

B.rationale: Confused supporters would not have rallied so quickly.

C.rationale: The speech did not change how many opponents there were; it changed the supporters' resolve.

hints: How did the supporters change after the speech?

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It offers evidence that the wall is longer than most people realize.
choices.B: It describes the conditions under which astronauts first photographed the wall.
choices.C: It explains why the wall is hard to see despite its great length.
choices.D: It introduces a comparison that the final sentence then rejects.

candidates.evidence: Although the wall is extremely long, it is only a few meters wide
candidates.explanation: The third sentence grants the wall's great length ('Although...') but explains, through its narrow width and matching color, why it is still hard to see, accounting for the astronauts' report.

A.rationale: The sentence uses the wall's length as a concession, not as a new claim about it.

B.rationale: No photographs or conditions are described.

D.rationale: The final sentence supports the comparison by naming structures that are easier to see.

hints: What does 'Although' concede, and what follows it?

strategy.explanation: Describe what the sentence does relative to the one before it.

candidates.remember: A sentence that begins with 'Although' often explains a surprising result.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: trees beside salmon streams absorb nitrogen directly from ocean water.
choices.B: salmon carried inland by bears may bring ocean nutrients to streamside forests.
choices.C: bears grow faster when they live near streams that salmon return to.
choices.D: salmon return to rivers because the streamside forests provide nutrients.

candidates.evidence: a form of nitrogen that is common in the ocean but rare on land
candidates.explanation: Ocean-type nitrogen shows up in streamside trees, which grow faster where salmon run; bears carry salmon into the woods. Together these suggest the salmon bring ocean nutrients to the forest.

A.rationale: The trees grow beside streams, not in the ocean; the text points to salmon carcasses as the carrier.

C.rationale: The text measures trees' growth, not bears'.

D.rationale: The text describes nutrients moving from salmon to trees, not the reverse.

hints: How could ocean nitrogen reach a tree on land?

strategy.explanation: Connect each fact to the next.

candidates.remember: Inference completions should link every clue the text gives.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researcher's conclusion?

choices.A: Virtual tours were taken by 38% of those 18–29 but only 14% of those 65 and older.
choices.B: In-person visits were made by 45% of those 18–29 and 55% of those 65 and older.
choices.C: Ages 50–64: 48% visited in person and 22% took a virtual tour of the museum.
choices.D: Ages 18–29: 45% in person and 38% virtual; ages 65 and older: 55% and 14%.

candidates.evidence: is much wider among the oldest visitors than among the youngest
candidates.explanation: Only D gives both measures for both the youngest and oldest groups. From D, the gap is 45 - 38 = 7 points for ages 18-29 and 55 - 14 = 41 points for 65 and older, much wider among the oldest.

A.rationale: This tracks only one of the two measures; the conclusion concerns the gap between them.

B.rationale: This tracks only in-person visits; the gap needs both measures.

C.rationale: This gives the gap for one group only, so it cannot show a difference between the youngest and oldest.

hints: What two numbers make up each gap?

strategy.explanation: Find the choice that lets you compute both gaps.

candidates.remember: A claim about a gap needs both measures in every group.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the linguists in Text 2 most likely respond to the critics' view in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the rise often invites a listener's response rather than signaling doubt
choices.B: By agreeing that the rise signals doubt, but only when speakers give directions
choices.C: By claiming that the rise is used mainly by speakers who are giving out lists of facts
choices.D: By suggesting that listeners rarely notice when a speaker's pitch rises at the end

candidates.evidence: the rise seems to work as a check, inviting the listener to signal that they are following
candidates.explanation: Text 1's critics read the rise as uncertainty; Text 2 finds it on statements speakers are sure of and explains it as a check on the listener, which disputes the critics' reading.

B.rationale: Text 2 says speakers use the rise on statements they are 'clearly sure of,' including directions.

C.rationale: Text 2 gives directions and facts as examples, not as the main use.

D.rationale: Text 2 says the rise invites listeners to respond, which implies they notice it.

hints: What does each text say the rise does?

strategy.explanation: State each text's view in a few words.

candidates.remember: Look for exactly where the second text disagrees with the first.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize how long the ravens waited between choosing the tool and using it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In some trials, ravens waited only 15 minutes before the box came back to them.
choices.B: Most ravens picked the useful tool from among several useless objects.
choices.C: Ravens that chose the tool with no box in sight used it up to 17 hours later.
choices.D: Planning for a future need, as these ravens did, is rare among animals.

candidates.explanation: The goal is the length of the wait. Only C states both events (choosing the tool and using it) and the gap of up to 17 hours between them.

A.rationale: This gives the shortest delay, which understates how long the ravens could wait.

B.rationale: This describes the choice but not the wait before using it.

D.rationale: This explains why the result matters but gives no time span.

hints: Which note gives a length of time?

strategy.explanation: Read the goal, then find the choice that includes the time span.

candidates.remember: Match the choice to the exact element the goal names.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: so the cars are not emission-free over their full lives
candidates.explanation: The first sentence states an advantage; the second qualifies it with a drawback. "Even so" signals that the advantage does not settle the matter.

B.rationale: Having no tailpipe emissions does not cause battery manufacturing to use fossil fuels.

C.rationale: Emissions from battery-making are a contrast to 'no tailpipe emissions,' not a similar point.

D.rationale: The second sentence adds a new fact rather than restating the first.

hints: Does the second sentence agree with or qualify the first?
candidates.remember: A concession transition admits one point, then limits it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: peat cutters found the Tollund Man's body
choices.C: there was the Tollund Man's body,
choices.D: the people who found the Tollund Man's body thought it was

candidates.evidence: Excavated from a peat bog in Denmark in 1950,
candidates.explanation: The introductory phrase describes something excavated from a bog, so the subject that follows must be the body: "the Tollund Man's body was so well preserved...."

A.rationale: The opening phrase describes what was excavated, so it must be followed by the body, not the investigators.

C.rationale: The phrase must modify a noun subject; 'there was' leaves it dangling.

D.rationale: This makes the people, not the body, the thing excavated from the bog.

hints: What was excavated from the bog?

strategy.explanation: Put the thing the opening phrase describes right after the comma.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier must be followed by the noun it describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: repairs to its suspension cables took longer than engineers expected
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses, so a semicolon must separate them, and the conjunctive adverb "however" that begins the second clause is followed by a comma.

A.rationale: A comma before "however" creates a comma splice between two independent clauses.

B.rationale: With no punctuation before "however," the two clauses run together.

C.rationale: "However" at the start of a clause should be followed by a comma.

hints: Can each part stand alone as a sentence?

strategy.explanation: Find the boundary between the two clauses.

candidates.remember: Use a semicolon before and a comma after "however" between clauses.
